chapter_or_section: Section "Jesus and God" (paragraph 58 of the web text; no headings in that paragraph)
page: page unknown (article pp. 42–56 of Ex Auditu 14; the web reproduction has no internal page numbers)
quote_orig: Jesus believed he would win the messianic victory over the real enemy and would build the true messianic temple through taking Israel’s fate upon himself and going to the cross. Jesus believed that in doing so he was not just pointing to or talking about, but was actually embodying, the return of YHWH to Zion.
context_before: When we do so, we find that dozens and dozens of lines of inquiry converge to produce a well ordered, coherent, historically credible sense of vocation, emerging in central symbolic actions, hinted at in a hundred cryptic and teasing sayings.
what_it_says: Wright argues that Jesus understood his vocation as actually embodying the return of YHWH to Zion, as a historical reconstruction of Jesus' own sense of vocation.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself acts as YHWH (partly; Wright says it is about what Jesus believed about his vocation, not a formula of identity); (B) portrayal of Jesus sharing YHWH's role
scholar_qualification: Wright does not say Jesus "knew he was God" in a trinitarian sense (see J6W-02 qualification). He says the historical claim is about vocation and that Jesus did not think of himself as "God" in that way. He also says the question of identity with God is separate: "this tells us nothing about whether he believed himself to be in any sense identified with Israel’s God" (para 62, same essay, see notes).

quote_orig: And Jesus seems to have believed it about himself. The language was deeply coded, but the symbolic action was not. He was coming to Zion, doing what YHWH had promised to do. He explained his action with riddles all pointing in the same direction.
context_before: To say that someone would share God’s throne was to say that, through this one, Israel’s God would win the great decisive victory. This is what, after all, the great Rabbi Akiba seems to have believed about bar-Kochba.
what_it_says: Wright says Jesus acted as one coming to Zion to do what YHWH had promised, and that Jesus believed himself called to do what in scripture only Israel's God did (sentence in same paragraph: "He believed himself called to do and be what in the scriptures only Israel’s God did and was.").
claim_supported: (A) Jesus speaks and acts as YHWH (Wright's formulation, historical reconstruction); (B) Gospel portrait
scholar_qualification: Wright explicitly denies the naive version: "I do not think Jesus “knew he was God” in the same sense that one knows one is tired or happy, male or female. He did not sit back and say to himself “Well I never! I’m the second person of the Trinity!”" (para 69, same essay). He says the claim is that Jesus believed he had to do and be what only YHWH could do, and he calls it a category of "vocation".

page: page unknown (article pp. 42–56 of Ex Auditu 14; the web reproduction has no internal page numbers)
quote_orig: Judaism spoke of the presence of her God in her midst, in the pillar of cloud and fire, in the Presence (“Shekinah”) in the Temple. Jesus acted and spoke as if he thought he were a one-man counter-temple movement.
context_before: Judaism had two great incarnational symbols. Temple and Torah: Jesus seems to have believed it was his vocation to upstage the one and outflank the other.
what_it_says: Wright argues that Jesus' temple actions and words make sense only if he acted as the place of God's presence, something Judaism reserved for God, so that the "Shekinah glory turns out to have a human face" (same paragraph).
claim_supported: (A) Jesus acts as the presence of YHWH (Temple); (B) Gospel portrayal; (E) the temple claim is about Jesus' vocation, not a titles argument
scholar_qualification: Wright does not argue from titles: "It cannot be read off from the usage of any “titles” such as “son of God” or “son of man.”" (para 62). He introduces the Temple material as "from another angle" (para 67), i.e. one of several lines of argument and that the claim is historical, not a claim that Jesus used trinitarian language.

quote_orig: It is this that also accounts for his sovereign attitude to Torah, his speaking on behalf of Wisdom, and his announcement of forgiveness of sins.[37] By themselves none of these would be conclusive. Even if they are allowed to stand as words and actions of Jesus, they remain cryptic.
context_before: Why, after all, does Jesus tell a story about a yearning father in order to account for his own behavior?[36]
what_it_says: Wright lists Jesus' announcement of forgiveness of sins among actions that, on his reading, fit the same vocation of YHWH returning to Zion, but says that taken alone they do not prove the point.
claim_supported: (A) partly: forgiveness of sins is listed as one of several actions; (E) cumulative argument
scholar_qualification: Wright does NOT, in this essay, analyse Mark 2:1-12, the Son of Man or the Lord of the Sabbath (see notes). The forgiveness point is one item in a cumulative case and Wright calls each item cryptic on its own. Footnote [37] cites Jacob Neusner’s interview remark, not Wright’s own argument.

quote_orig: Isaiah has YHWH defeating the pagan idols and being enthroned over them: Paul has Jesus exalted to a position of equality with “the Father” because he has done what, in Jewish tradition, only the one God can do.
context_before: Paul this time draws on the fiercely monotheistic theology of Isaiah 40-55 to celebrate Christ’s universal lordship: “At the name of Jesus”, he declares, “every knee shall bow.”
what_it_says: Wright says Paul portrays the exalted Jesus as sharing the Father's position because Jesus did what, in Jewish tradition, only the one God does.
claim_supported: (B) the Gospels/earliest Christians portray Jesus as sharing YHWH's unique identity (Paul, not Jesus' own words); (C) early worship of Jesus
scholar_qualification: This is Wright's account of Paul, not of Jesus' self-understanding. Wright separates the two in this essay (see para 62: "continuity though not identity").

quote_orig: In 1 Corinthians 8:6, within a specifically Jewish-style monotheistic argument, he adapts the Shema itself, placing Jesus within it: “For us there is one God—the Father, from whom are all things and we to him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him.” This is possibly the single most revolutionary christological formulation in the whole of early Christianity, staking out a high christology founded within the very citadel of Jewish monotheism.
context_before: Within that strand of material, three passages stand out.[19]
what_it_says: Wright says 1 Corinthians 8:6 places Jesus inside the Shema, which he calls possibly the most revolutionary christological formulation of early Christianity.
claim_supported: (B) earliest Christians portray Jesus within YHWH's unique identity; (C) early Christian worship/monotheism
scholar_qualification: Wright treats this as the early church's reformulation of Jewish monotheism, not as Jesus' own words (the essay argues Jesus' vocation is the historical starting point, para 58). He treats the Shema reformulation as a Pauline text, not a quotation of Jesus.
